clue.text: Stole it? Unfortunately an understatement

indicators.note: things gone unfortunately have gone wrong, so the letters of the two words before it are put in a fresh order

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether a thing was stolen, and the reply plays the matter down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Unfortunately' rearranges STOLEIT into the answer, a figure of speech that affirms by denying the opposite ('not bad').
explanation.definitionFit: This is the rhetorical figure of deliberate understatement, as in saying 'not bad' to mean very good.

clue.text: Illumination 'makes one yellowish-green and faint

parts.note: lime is a yellowish-green colour
faint means slight, as in a light touch

explanation.surface: A lamp gives off a pale yellow-green glow.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer was the intense white stage light made by heating quicklime.
explanation.definitionFit: It was the bright stage lighting of Victorian theatres, made by heating quicklime.

clue.text: Special gifts of old coins

explanation.definitionFit: The word means natural aptitudes, and also the ancient weights of silver used as money in the Bible's parable.

clue.text: State that's first to acquire eight points

indicators.note: first takes the opening letter of the word that follows

parts.note: eight compass points: E, N, N, E, S, S, E, E

explanation.surface: A state is the first to win eight points.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'points' are compass points, which give the letters E, N and S.
explanation.definitionFit: This is one of the United States, home of Nashville.

clue.text: Cleaner helping to dress OAP

indicators.note: a helping is a portion, here a portion of the words that follow

explanation.surface: Something that cleans helps to get a pensioner dressed.
explanation.walkthrough: OAP is British for old-age pensioner; the answer is a portion of 'dress OAP'.
explanation.definitionFit: It is the everyday washing agent made from fats and alkali.

clue.text: Bills for a man in poor health

parts.note: someone in poor health is sick
Les is a man's name, short for Leslie

explanation.surface: Invoices are made out to a man who is unwell.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bills' looks like invoices but means cutting tools: a bill or billhook is a curved blade, close kin to a reaping hook.
explanation.definitionFit: A bill is an old hooked cutting blade, and these curved reaping blades belong to the same family of tools.

clue.text: Used this to mark the ticks

explanation.definitionFit: It means previously owned, and is also the pointer on a clock face that counts off the seconds.

clue.text: Daughter surrounded by, attention from basic training unit

indicators.note: surrounded by puts the daughter inside the word for attention

parts.note: care is close attention

explanation.surface: A girl gets close attention from the people who give basic training.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer is a nucleus of trained people round whom a larger force can be built.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a small core group of trained personnel around which a larger organisation is formed.

clue.text: Gentle man, that is, not heartless

parts.note: Len is a man's name

indicators.note: heartless removes the central letter of the word not

explanation.surface: A gentle man is, it seems, not heartless.
explanation.walkthrough: 'heartless' takes the middle O out of NOT to leave NT.
explanation.definitionFit: Merciful, mild, not strict.

clue.text: Kid won over: in conversation

indicators.note: in conversation means the word is as spoken, so a word of the same sound

parts.note: someone won over has been swayed

explanation.surface: A child is persuaded during a chat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Kid' is not a child but kid leather; the answer is a soft napped leather, often of kid.
explanation.definitionFit: Kidskin can be given this soft napped finish, so the two are both soft leathers.

clue.text: Writer detailed to include, a place in Italy

indicators.note: to include signals that the shortened name takes a letter inside it
de-tailed, with its tail or last letter cut off, applied to the writer's name

parts.note: A. A. Milne, the author of Winnie-the-Pooh

explanation.surface: An author is sent off on assignment to cover a town in Italy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'detailed' reads as assigned but means 'tail removed': MILNE loses E to give MILN, and 'to include' puts A inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: This northern Italian city is the capital of Lombardy.

clue.text: Changes in the form of words-they are not expected in speech

definitions.text: Changes in the form of words

indicators.note: in speech says the words are heard spoken, giving a word of the same sound

parts.note: accidents are events nobody expects

explanation.surface: A grammar note says that inflected forms are not what we expect when we talk.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer is the old grammar term for inflection; spoken aloud it is indistinguishable from 'accidents'.
explanation.definitionFit: In grammar this is the part dealing with inflection, the endings and changes a word takes for case, tense or number.

clue.text: Cavalry man not finishing the dance

indicators.note: not finishing means the last letter of the dance's name is dropped

parts.note: the Lancers is a nineteenth-century square dance, a kind of quadrille

explanation.surface: A mounted soldier leaves a ball before the dance is over.
explanation.walkthrough: The Lancers, a quadrille, loses its final S; the result is a soldier armed with a lance.
explanation.definitionFit: A soldier of a cavalry regiment originally armed with lances.

clue.text: Come first against a good player, say

indicators.note: say signals that the words are judged by their sound

parts.note: against is ANTI, and a good tennis player is a seed, together ANTI-SEED

explanation.surface: To get ahead, one must take on a strong opponent.
explanation.walkthrough: In tennis a seed is a highly ranked player; ANTI plus SEED spoken aloud gives the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: To precede, go before in time or order.

clue.text: I have a way with this investor

parts.note: the letter I as printed is a capital, so it reads as CAPITAL I
St is the abbreviation for street, a way

explanation.surface: Someone claims to have found a route to make money with this backer.
explanation.walkthrough: The trick is seeing the 'I' as a capital letter, read as words; 'have', 'a' and 'with this' are joining words.
explanation.definitionFit: This person puts money into business for profit.

clue.text: Puffs cigarettes without hesitation

indicators.note: without tells us the hesitation sound is taken out of the cigarettes

parts.note: gaspers is old British slang for cheap cigarettes
er is the sound of a speaker hesitating

explanation.surface: A smoker draws on cigarettes without pausing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Puffs' looks like smoking but means pants for breath; GASPERS, British slang for cigarettes, loses ER.
explanation.definitionFit: Both mean short sharp breaths drawn in when winded.

clue.text: With no leitmotif, science has no ends

indicators.note: has no ends means the first and last letters of the science are removed

parts.note: mathematics is a science

explanation.surface: A remark that a theme-free piece of music is like a science without purpose.
explanation.walkthrough: MATHEMATICS loses its first and last letters. In music the answer describes writing not built on recurring themes.
explanation.definitionFit: A musical term for a piece not developed from themes, so lacking any recurring motif.

clue.text: Building semi — not a detached initially — on the Medway

indicators.note: building means constructing, so the letters are put together in a new way
initially takes the first letter of the word detached

explanation.surface: A semi-detached house is going up beside a Kent river.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Building' rearranges SEMI, NOT, A and D. The Medway is a river in Kent, south-east England, and the answer is Kent's county town on it.
explanation.definitionFit: The county town of Kent stands on the banks of this river.

clue.text: Mathematical function into which, oddly, ten can't go

indicators.note: oddly means arranged in a strange way, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A function into which ten cannot be divided.
explanation.walkthrough: 'oddly' suggests odd letters, but here it rearranges TENCANTGO.
explanation.definitionFit: A trigonometric ratio, the reciprocal of the tangent.

clue.text: Sarah Bernhardt represents a radiant example

indicators.note: represents in the sense of re-presents, setting the letters out anew

parts.note: e.g. is the usual abbreviation for 'for example'

explanation.surface: The great French actress is held up as a shining model.
explanation.walkthrough: 'represents' rearranges RADIANT plus EG. Sarah Bernhardt was a celebrated French actress famed for tragic roles, so she is an instance of the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: She was a famous actress of tragic roles, an example of a performer in serious drama.

clue.text: Evangelist, a 26 with the French

parts.note: 26 across is SITUATION, here in its sense of a job, a post
le is French for 'the'

explanation.surface: A preacher holds a position that comes with French.
explanation.walkthrough: The number refers to another clue's answer in the job sense.
explanation.definitionFit: Each of the twelve sent out by Jesus to spread the gospel, or any zealous advocate.

clue.text: "The — who praises, with enthusiastic tone' (Gilbert)

parts.note: a fill-in from Ko-Ko's 'little list' song in Gilbert and Sullivan's The Mikado, naming the fool who praises every century but this one

explanation.surface: A gap in a line from W. S. Gilbert's lyrics.
explanation.walkthrough: The full line runs on 'all centuries but this, and every country but his own'.
explanation.definitionFit: In The Mikado the fool who praises all centuries but his own is named in this line by the word for a dunce.

clue.text: Repeat a note in one scale

indicators.note: in puts the note inside the other pieces

parts.note: one is I, the Roman numeral
rate is a scale of charges, as in rates of pay
te is the seventh note of the sol-fa scale

explanation.surface: A singer repeats a note within a single musical scale.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' places TE inside IRATE. 'scale' looks musical but means a rate.
explanation.definitionFit: To say or do again.

clue.text: Theatrical centre where the Method is all-embracing

parts.note: broad means wide-ranging, all-embracing
a way is a method of doing something

explanation.surface: New York's theatre district is where Method acting rules everything.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Method' looks like Method acting, but it is just a way of doing things; a broad way is the 'all-embracing' one.
explanation.definitionFit: This New York street is home to the city's major theatres.

clue.text: Fundamental notes thus produced…

parts.note: B and A are musical notes
sic is Latin for thus

explanation.surface: Basic notes are made this way, leading into the next clue.
explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis runs on to the next clue but plays no part in this one's wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Elementary, forming the base.

clue.text: …by a fly bird?

explanation.walkthrough: Read with the previous clue, the notes are quacks produced by a male duck.
explanation.definitionFit: Anglers use this name for the mayfly, and it is also the male duck.

clue.text: Behind Goodfellow in near-riot

indicators.note: in places the saint inside the jumbled letters
a riot of letters means they are thrown into disorder

parts.note: a saint is a good fellow, abbreviated ST

explanation.surface: Someone lags behind a man named Goodfellow during a near-riot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'riot' jumbles NEAR to AERN and 'in' puts ST inside it. 'Goodfellow' suggests Robin Goodfellow, but it is simply a good fellow, a saint.
explanation.definitionFit: A nautical word for at or towards the rear of a ship.

clue.text: Fixes up a bargain here

indicators.note: up in a down clue means the word is read from the bottom upwards

parts.note: pins fix things in place

explanation.surface: A shop fixes things and offers a good deal.
explanation.walkthrough: In this down clue 'up' sends PINS backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: In British slang a cheap purchase, a steal.

clue.text: Place in a job

explanation.definitionFit: It can mean a location or setting, and also a post of employment.

clue.text: Like -Humpty-Dumpty, having no tax exemption 'initially

parts.note: no is nought, the letter O
VAT is value added tax, the British sales tax

indicators.note: initially takes the first letter of the word exemption

explanation.surface: The nursery-rhyme egg has no tax relief.
explanation.walkthrough: Humpty-Dumpty is an egg, so the answer means egg-shaped. VAT is Britain's sales tax.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means egg-shaped, and the nursery-rhyme character is pictured as an egg.

clue.text: The prime minister's fine

explanation.definitionFit: Attlee, the postwar British prime minister, had this first name; as an adjective it means mild, as fine weather is.

clue.text: Excuse before the beginning of the sermon

parts.note: pre- is the prefix meaning before
a preacher opens a sermon by announcing its text, the scripture passage it expounds

explanation.surface: A preacher pleads an excuse just before starting the sermon.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the beginning of the sermon' looks like a first letter, but it is the Bible verse a sermon starts from.
explanation.definitionFit: A false reason given to cover the real one.
